# Find a twin: how the matching works {#sec-twins-method}

```{r twins-method-setup}
#| include: false
source(here::here("R", "twins_data.R"))   # d, MNUM, MCAT, W, W_R2: exactly what twins.qmd uses
TW_LAB <- c(fsm = "Free school meals", ks2 = "KS2 prior attainment", eal = "English as an additional language",
            wbri = "White British", mobile = "Joined mid-phase", girls = "Girls", sen = "SEN support",
            ehcp = "EHC plans", semh = "Social, emotional and mental health need", l4z = "Neighbourhood education",
            size = "Size", place = "Rural or urban", adm = "Admissions", sixth = "Sixth form", faith = "Religious character")
TW_VARS <- c(MNUM, MCAT)
TW_SD <- sapply(MNUM, function(v) sd(d[[v]], na.rm = TRUE))
# The distance of every school from school i, as on the page (twins.js)
tw_dist <- function(i, wt) {
  tot <- 0; den <- 0
  for (v in MNUM) { g <- pmin(abs(d[[v]] - d[[v]][i]) / TW_SD[[v]] / 3, 1); ok <- !is.na(g)
    tot <- tot + ifelse(ok, wt[[v]] * g, 0); den <- den + ifelse(ok, wt[[v]], 0) }
  for (v in MCAT) { g <- as.numeric(d[[v]] != d[[v]][i]); ok <- !is.na(g)
    tot <- tot + ifelse(ok, wt[[v]] * g, 0); den <- den + ifelse(ok, wt[[v]], 0) }
  out <- tot / den; out[i] <- NA; out
}
W_EQ <- setNames(as.list(rep(1, length(TW_VARS))), TW_VARS)

# ---- worked example: Dorothy Stringer and its closest twin on the results weights ----
ex_i <- which(d$n == "Dorothy Stringer School")[1]
ex_d <- tw_dist(ex_i, W$att8); ex_j <- which.min(ex_d)
ex_show <- function(v, i) { x <- d[[v]][i]
  if (v == "size") return(format(round(exp(x)), big.mark = ","))
  if (v == "l4z") return(sprintf("%.2f SD (%.0f%% level 4+)", x, d$l4[i]))
  if (is.numeric(x)) return(sprintf("%.1f", x)); as.character(x) }
ex <- tibble(v = TW_VARS) |>
  mutate(Characteristic = TW_LAB[v],
         a = sapply(v, ex_show, i = ex_i), b = sapply(v, ex_show, i = ex_j),
         gap_sd = sapply(v, function(k) if (k %in% MNUM) abs(d[[k]][ex_i] - d[[k]][ex_j]) / TW_SD[[k]] else NA_real_),
         g = sapply(v, function(k) if (k %in% MNUM) min(abs(d[[k]][ex_i] - d[[k]][ex_j]) / TW_SD[[k]] / 3, 1)
                                    else as.numeric(d[[k]][ex_i] != d[[k]][ex_j])),
         w = unlist(W$att8[v]), part = w * g)
ex_dist <- sum(ex$part) / sum(ex$w)
ex_eq <- 100 * (1 - tw_dist(ex_i, W_EQ)[ex_j])
ex_rank_eq <- rank(tw_dist(ex_i, W_EQ), na.last = "keep")[ex_j]

# ---- checks: do twins on intake have like results? -----------------------------
# For every school, the mean of its ten closest twins (England) against its own value
set.seed(20261112)
check <- function(wt, y, n = 10) {
  nb <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(d)), function(i) { di <- tw_dist(i, wt); mean(y[order(di)[seq_len(n)]], na.rm = TRUE) })
  rnd <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(d)), function(i) mean(y[sample(setdiff(seq_len(nrow(d)), i), n)], na.rm = TRUE))
  c(twins = cor(y, nb, use = "complete.obs"), random = cor(y, rnd, use = "complete.obs"))
}
labs_y <- c(att8 = "Attainment 8", overall = "Overall absence (log)")
chk <- bind_rows(
  tibble(measure = labs_y[["att8"]], weights = c("Weighted for results", "Equal"),
         r = c(check(W$att8, d$att8)[["twins"]], check(W_EQ, d$att8)[["twins"]])),
  tibble(measure = labs_y[["overall"]], weights = c("Weighted for overall absence", "Equal"),
         r = c(check(W$overall, log(d$overall + 0.1))[["twins"]], check(W_EQ, log(d$overall + 0.1))[["twins"]])))
rnd_att8 <- check(W_EQ, d$att8)[["random"]]
closest_sim <- 100 * (1 - sapply(seq_len(nrow(d)), function(i) min(tw_dist(i, W$att8), na.rm = TRUE)))
```

[Find a twin](twins.qmd), the [School Information System](simulator.qmd)'s
Find My Twin tab, and the trust pages all start from the same idea. Describe
every state-funded secondary school by its intake and setting. Measure how
far apart two schools are on those characteristics. Then show the schools
nearest to a chosen school, its *twins*, beside it. Results and attendance
are never used to choose twins, only to compare them once chosen, so a twin
is a school facing a similar task, not one getting similar results. This
section sets out the data, the distance, the weights and a worked example,
and checks how far matching on intake brings like results. The code is
`R/twins_data.R` (data and weights, shared by the page and this section) and
`twins.js` (the matching in the browser); the app repeats it in
`app/R/mod_twin.R`.

## The characteristics {#sec-twins-data}

There are `r nrow(d)` schools with every characteristic and 2025/26 absence
(the set the [absence models](absence_causes.qmd) use). Each is described by
fifteen characteristics in four groups, each of which the page lets you
switch off:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-twins-vars
#| tbl-cap: "The fifteen matching characteristics: what each is, where it comes from, and its spread across schools (the standard deviation that scales its gaps)."
src <- c(fsm = "School census, January 2026", ks2 = "KS4 performance tables (latest model year)",
         eal = "School census, January 2026", wbri = "School census, January 2026",
         mobile = "KS4 performance tables (latest model year)", girls = "School census, January 2026",
         sen = "SEN in England, January 2026", ehcp = "SEN in England, January 2026",
         semh = "SEN in England, January 2026", l4z = "Census 2021 (TS067), 150 nearest Output Areas",
         size = "School census, January 2026", place = "School census (2021 rural-urban classification)",
         adm = "KS4 performance tables (latest model year)", sixth = "KS4 performance tables (oldest age taught, latest model year)",
         faith = "School census, January 2026")
what <- c(fsm = "% of pupils known to be eligible for free school meals",
          ks2 = "Mean KS2 scaled score of the KS4 cohort, minus 100",
          eal = "% whose first language is known or believed to be other than English",
          wbri = "% of pupils of White British ethnic origin", mobile = "% of the KS4 cohort who joined mid-phase",
          girls = "% of pupils who are girls", sen = "% of pupils on SEN support", ehcp = "% of pupils with an EHC plan",
          semh = "% with social, emotional and mental health as their primary need (support or plan)",
          l4z = "Adults with level 4+ qualifications, standardised", size = "Pupils on roll (log)",
          place = "Urban near a major town or city; urban further from one; rural",
          adm = "Selective; non-selective; non-selective in a highly selective area",
          sixth = "Has a sixth form, or 11-16", faith = "Has a religious character, or not")
tibble(v = TW_VARS) |>
  transmute(Group = c(rep("Pupils", 6), rep("Needs", 3), "Neighbourhood and place", "The school", "Neighbourhood and place", rep("The school", 3)),
            Characteristic = TW_LAB[v], Definition = what[v], Source = src[v],
            Type = ifelse(v %in% MNUM, "Measured", "Category"),
            `SD across schools` = ifelse(v %in% MNUM, sprintf("%.2f", TW_SD[v]), "")) |>
  arrange(factor(Group, c("Pupils", "Needs", "Neighbourhood and place", "The school"))) |>
  kt(align = "llllcr")
```

The census and SEN figures are the school's own, from January 2026, the
nearest in time to the 2025/26 absence they are compared with. KS2 prior
attainment, mobility, neighbourhood education and admissions are the Value
Added v2.1 inputs for the school's latest model year (`R/01_inputs.R`; see
[the variables](#sec-full-spec)). A school that changed URN is matched on
either number. Free school meals here is current eligibility from the
census, not the FSM6 (ever in six years) measure the value-added model
uses, so the twins' figures can differ a little from the school's other
pages.

## The distance {#sec-twins-distance}

For two schools *a* and *b*, each characteristic *k* gives a gap between 0
(the same) and 1 (as different as it can count):

$$
g_k(a,b) = \begin{cases}
\min\!\left(\dfrac{|x_{ak} - x_{bk}|}{3\,s_k},\ 1\right) & \text{a measured characteristic, } s_k \text{ its standard deviation across schools}\\[1.2ex]
0 \text{ if } x_{ak} = x_{bk},\ 1 \text{ otherwise} & \text{a category}
\end{cases}
$$

The distance is the weighted average of the gaps, over the characteristics
both schools have, and similarity is its complement as a percentage:

$$
D(a,b) = \frac{\sum_k w_k\, g_k(a,b)}{\sum_k w_k}, \qquad \text{similarity} = 100\,\big(1 - D(a,b)\big).
$$

This is a form of Gower's distance, as in the original project's twin
finder, with one change: a measured gap is scaled by the standard deviation
rather than the range. The range is set by the two most extreme schools in
England, so a single outlier would squash every other gap. Capping at three
standard deviations means a gap that large counts as a complete mismatch,
the same as a different category, and no one characteristic can dominate.

## The weights {#sec-twins-weights}

With equal weights, a match on religious character counts as much as a
match on prior attainment. But characteristics matter very differently for
results and for absence, so by default each is weighted by how much it moves
the measure being compared. For each measure *y* (Attainment 8, or the log
of a kind of absence), one ordinary least-squares regression across schools
on all fifteen characteristics:

$$
y_s = \beta_0 + \sum_{k} \beta_k\, x_{sk} + \varepsilon_s ,
$$

```r
m <- lm(y ~ fsm + ks2 + eal + wbri + mobile + girls + sen + ehcp + semh + l4z + size +
          place + adm + sixth + faith, data = d)
w_raw <- apply(predict(m, type = "terms"), 2, sd)   # SD across schools of each fitted part
w <- pmax(w_raw / mean(w_raw), 0.05)                # average one; nothing quite ignored
```

The weight of a characteristic is the standard deviation, across schools, of
its fitted part of the measure ($\hat\beta_k x_{sk}$, or the sum of a
category's terms). So a characteristic counts for a lot if it both moves the
measure strongly and varies a lot between schools. The weights are scaled to
average one, with a floor of 0.05. The regression is only a ruler for
importance: it is not used to predict anything, and its coefficients are not
reported as effects. Value added and the Attainment 8 of each group take the
Attainment 8 weights, because value added is what is left once intake is
allowed for, so twins for it should match on what drives results. The
combined measure (absence and value added together) averages the overall
absence and Attainment 8 weights.

```{r}
#| label: fig-twins-weights
#| fig-cap: "Matching weights for results and for three kinds of absence (average one). A dashed line marks equal weighting. The R² under each panel's title is how much of the measure the fifteen characteristics explain between schools."
#| fig-height: 6.2
wl <- c(att8 = "Results (Att8, value added)", overall = "Overall absence", unauth = "Unauthorised absence",
        persistent = "Persistent absence")
wd <- bind_rows(lapply(names(wl), function(o) tibble(measure = sprintf("%s\nR² %.0f%%", wl[[o]], 100 * W_R2[[o]]),
                                                      v = TW_VARS, w = unlist(W[[o]][TW_VARS])))) |>
  mutate(lab = factor(TW_LAB[v], rev(TW_LAB[TW_VARS])), measure = factor(measure, unique(measure)))
ggplot(wd, aes(w, lab)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = GREY) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = w, yend = lab), colour = LPURPLE, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(colour = DPURPLE, size = 2.4) + facet_wrap(~measure, nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = "Weight", y = NULL) + theme_note(11)
```

For results, prior attainment carries by far the most weight
(`r sprintf("%.1f", W$att8$ks2)`), then disadvantage, admissions (a
selective school differs most) and neighbourhood education. For overall
absence the White British share, disadvantage and prior attainment lead,
then mobility and social, emotional and mental health need, while
neighbourhood education and size count for little. For unauthorised
absence, disadvantage dominates (`r sprintf("%.1f", W$unauth$fsm)`). The full table of weights for every measure,
including illness and severe absence, is on [the page](twins.qmd#sec-how).

## Choosing the twins {#sec-twins-choose}

Every other school's similarity to the chosen school is worked out, within
England, the same region, or everywhere outside the school's own authority.

- **Closest twins** are the most similar schools.
- **Anti-twins** ("look-alikes doing better") come from a pool of the 25, 50
  or 100 most similar schools: those that do better than the chosen school
  on the measure (lower absence, higher Attainment 8 or value added),
  ordered by how much better. The pool keeps them similar; the ordering
  picks out the biggest differences among similar schools.

Across England, the median school's closest twin (results weights) has a
similarity of `r pts(median(closest_sim), 0)`; nine in ten schools have a
twin above `r pts(quantile(closest_sim, 0.1), 0)`.

## A worked example {#sec-twins-example}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-twins-example
#| tbl-cap: !expr 'paste0("How similar ", d$n[ex_j], " is to ", d$n[ex_i], ", with the results weights: each characteristic, its gap, and its weighted part of the distance.")'
ex |> transmute(Characteristic, !!d$n[ex_i] := a, !!d$n[ex_j] := b,
                `Gap (SDs)` = ifelse(is.na(gap_sd), "", sprintf("%.2f", gap_sd)),
                `Gap counted, g` = sprintf("%.3f", g), `Weight, w` = sprintf("%.2f", w), `w × g` = sprintf("%.3f", part)) |>
  bind_rows(tibble(Characteristic = "<b>Total</b>", `Weight, w` = sprintf("<b>%.2f</b>", sum(ex$w)),
                   `w × g` = sprintf("<b>%.3f</b>", sum(ex$part)))) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), ~ coalesce(.x, ""))) |>
  kt(escape = FALSE, align = "lllrrrr")
```

The closest twin of `r d$n[ex_i]` (`r d$la[ex_i]`) across England, matched
for results, is `r d$n[ex_j]` (`r d$la[ex_j]`). Taking one row: a measured
characteristic's gap is the difference divided by its standard deviation,
then by three, and capped at one; a category's gap is 0 or 1. Each gap is
multiplied by its weight. The weighted gaps sum to `r sprintf("%.3f", sum(ex$part))`
and the weights to `r sprintf("%.2f", sum(ex$w))`, so the distance is
`r sprintf("%.3f", sum(ex$part))` / `r sprintf("%.2f", sum(ex$w))` =
`r sprintf("%.3f", ex_dist)` and the similarity is 100 × (1 −
`r sprintf("%.3f", ex_dist)`) = **`r pts(100 * (1 - ex_dist), 1)`**. With
equal weights the same pair is `r pts(ex_eq, 1)` similar, and
`r d$n[ex_j]` is `r ord(ex_rank_eq)` closest rather than first: the weights
reward matching on what drives results.

## Do twins on intake have like results? {#sec-twins-checks}

If the matching works, a school's twins should have results and absence
like its own, even though neither was used to choose them. For every
school, the mean of its ten closest twins in England is set against the
school's own value:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-twins-checks
#| tbl-cap: "Correlation across schools between a school's own value and the mean of its ten closest twins (England). Ten schools drawn at random give a correlation near zero."
chk |> transmute(Measure = measure, `Twins chosen with` = weights, `Correlation with own value` = sprintf("%.2f", r)) |>
  kt(align = "llr")
```

Ten random schools give `r sprintf("%.2f", rnd_att8)` for Attainment 8. Twins
chosen on intake alone track a school's results closely, a little more so
with the results weights than with equal weights; absence is harder to
predict from intake, as its lower R² says, so twins' absence is a looser
guide. The weights matter more for *which* schools come out as twins (in
the example above, the closest twin for results is only the
`r ord(ex_rank_eq)` closest with equal weights) than for how alike the
twins are on average. What the twins do not share is what is left: the part of a
school's results or absence its intake does not account for, which is where
a comparison with a twin is useful.

## What the matching cannot do {#sec-twins-limits}

- **Similar is not identical.** Twins can differ in what the data do not
  see: pupils' health, the community, buildings, staffing, history.
- **A better twin is a question, not an answer.** An anti-twin that does
  much better is a reason to ask what it does differently, not proof that
  copying it would work, and some of the difference will be chance.
- **One point in time.** The characteristics are January 2026 (and the
  latest model year); a school whose intake is changing fast may match
  different schools next year.
- **Absence is 2025/26 autumn and spring**, so the set is schools with
  absence published for those terms.

**In the School Information System.** The app's Find My Twin tab uses the
same schools, characteristics, standard deviations and distance, with three
weightings: for results, for overall absence, or equal. It compares twins on
value added and Attainment 8 for the pupil group and period chosen in the
app, and on absence against expected; its pool and number of twins are
sliders.
